title: Macroeconomics: Government Budget and the Economy

topics.title: The budget and the allocation function

learn.hook: Nobody sells tickets to street lights or national defence. If the market won't provide them, who will? Enter the government budget.
points: The government budget is an annual financial statement of the estimated receipts and expenditure of the government for a financial year (1 April to 31 March). Article 112 of the Constitution calls it the 'Annual Financial Statement'.
Allocation function: the government provides public goods that the market fails to supply in enough quantity, such as defence, roads, street lighting and public administration.
Public goods are non-rivalrous (one person's use does not reduce another's) and non-excludable (people who do not pay cannot easily be kept out).
Free-rider problem: since non-payers cannot be excluded, people avoid paying, so private firms cannot collect enough revenue. Hence the government provides public goods, financed by taxes.
Private goods (food, clothes, cars) are rivalrous and excludable and are supplied through markets.

example.q: Classify as public or private goods: (i) a lighthouse; (ii) a pizza; (iii) national defence; (iv) a seat in a cinema hall.
steps: Ask: is it non-rivalrous and non-excludable?
Lighthouse: ships cannot be kept from seeing it, and one ship's use doesn't reduce another's → public
Defence: protects everyone at once → public
Pizza and a cinema seat: one person's use excludes another's, and non-payers can be kept out → private

learn.reallife: Every February, the Union Finance Minister presents the Union Budget in Parliament, setting out how much will be spent on defence, railways, health and more.

quiz.q: The government budget is a statement of

Answer: Because of the free-rider problem, private firms cannot collect enough payment

quiz.q: Which is an example of a public good?
quiz.explain: Defence protects everyone at once and non-payers cannot be excluded.

A ticket, a bag and coffee are rival and excludable (private)
Answer: National defence
quiz.mistake: Thinks goods sold by the government are public goods

quiz.q: Providing public goods is the budget's
quiz.explain: Allocation of resources to public goods is the allocation function.
steps: Providing public goods like defence and roads allocates resources to them
That is the allocation function
Answer: allocation function
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the three functions

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Markets fail to provide public goods in sufficient quantity. Reason (R): Public goods are non-rivalrous and non-excludable, so consumers can avoid paying.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

R: public goods are non-rivalrous and non-excludable, so people avoid paying — true

quiz.q: A good that is rivalrous and excludable is a
quiz.explain: Rival and excludable goods are private goods sold in markets.

Such goods are sold in markets: private goods
Answer: private good
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the two features

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why can't a private company sell street lights to each person who walks below them?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Street lights are non-rivalrous and non-excludable, so everyone free-rides; that's why the government provides them!
teach.nudge: You said people won't pay. Why can't the company stop non-payers from using the light?

revise.summary: The budget is the government's annual statement of estimated receipts and expenditure (Article 112). Its allocation function provides public goods, which markets underprovide because they are non-rivalrous and non-excludable.
focus: Define the budget and the financial year
remember: Budget: 'Annual Financial Statement', Article 112, year 1 April–31 March
Public goods: non-rivalrous and non-excludable
Free-rider problem → government provides public goods
traps: Non-excludable is not the same as non-rivalrous
A cinema seat or bus ticket is a private good
The budget is an estimate, not actual figures

topics.title: Redistribution, stabilisation and the two budget accounts

learn.hook: A tax on high incomes funding free school meals, and extra spending on highways during a slowdown: two different jobs done by the same budget.
points: Redistribution function: the government changes the distribution of income through taxes and transfers (pensions, subsidies, scholarships), so that disposable income is fairer.
Stabilisation function: the government uses its spending and taxes to reduce fluctuations in output and employment; raising AD in a slump and lowering it during inflation.
Other objectives: promoting economic growth (e.g. capital spending on infrastructure) and managing public enterprises.
The budget has two parts: the revenue budget (revenue receipts and revenue expenditure) and the capital budget (capital receipts and capital expenditure).
Fiscal policy means the use of government spending and taxation to achieve these objectives.

example.q: Identify the budget function: (i) old-age pensions for poor elderly; (ii) extra spending on roads in a recession; (iii) building a defence radar system.
steps: (i) a transfer to reduce inequality → redistribution
(ii) raising AD to fight a slump → stabilisation
(iii) providing a public good → allocation

learn.reallife: Free foodgrain under the National Food Security Act and PM-KISAN transfers are examples of the redistribution function in India's budget.

games.title: Function and example
pairs: Providing national defence and street lighting

quiz.q: The redistribution function of the budget aims to

quiz.explain: Taxes on the rich and transfers to the poor make disposable income fairer.

Taxes (especially on the rich) and transfers (pensions, subsidies) make disposable income fairer
Answer: make the distribution of income fairer through taxes and transfers
quiz.mistake: Confuses redistribution with allocation

quiz.q: Raising government spending during a recession is an example of the
quiz.explain: It aims to smooth fluctuations in output and employment.
steps: Spending more in a recession raises AD
Smoothing ups and downs in output and jobs is the stabilisation function
Answer: stabilisation function
quiz.mistake: Thinks all spending is allocation

quiz.q: The two parts of the government budget are
quiz.explain: The budget is divided into revenue and capital accounts.
steps: The budget has a revenue part and a capital part
Revenue budget: revenue receipts and expenditure; capital budget: capital receipts and expenditure
Answer: revenue budget and capital budget
quiz.mistake: Confuses the budget with the balance of payments

quiz.q: Which is a transfer payment used for redistribution?
quiz.explain: Transfers are payments without any service in return.
steps: Transfer payment = payment without any service in return
Unemployment allowance is such a payment; a soldier's salary is for a service
Answer: Unemployment allowance

quiz.q: Which objective is served when the government invests heavily in railways and power plants?
quiz.explain: Capital spending raises productive capacity and growth.

Answer: Economic growth

quiz.q: The use of government spending and taxes to influence the economy is called
quiz.explain: Fiscal policy works through the budget; monetary policy is run by the RBI.
steps: Government spending and taxation are budget tools
Their use is fiscal policy (monetary policy is run by the RBI)
Answer: fiscal policy
quiz.mistake: Mixes up fiscal and monetary policy

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Progressive income taxes help the redistribution function. Reason (R): Under progressive taxation, people with higher incomes pay a higher rate of tax.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Taking a larger share from the rich and spending on the poor reduces inequality.
steps: A: progressive taxes help redistribution — true
R: higher incomes pay higher tax rates — true
Taking a larger share from the rich reduces inequality: R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not connect higher rates on the rich to redistribution

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Stabilisation means the government always increases its spending. Reason (R): Stabilisation aims to reduce fluctuations in output and employment.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: During inflation the government cuts spending or raises taxes, so A is false; R is true.
steps: In inflation, stabilisation means cutting spending or raising taxes, so A is false
R: stabilisation aims to reduce fluctuations — true
Answer: A is false, but R is true
quiz.mistake: Thinks stabilisation only means expansion

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does the government budget do so many jobs? What are they?'
teach.praise: Tweet! The budget allocates (public goods), redistributes (taxes and transfers), stabilises (smooths booms and slumps), and has revenue and capital parts!
teach.nudge: You've named one job. What about reducing inequality and smoothing out booms and slumps?

revise.summary: Beyond allocation, the budget redistributes income through taxes and transfers, stabilises output and employment, and promotes growth. It has a revenue budget and a capital budget, and using it this way is fiscal policy.
focus: Identify the budget function in an example
Name the two parts of the budget
remember: Functions: allocation, redistribution, stabilisation (and growth)
Two parts: revenue budget and capital budget
Fiscal policy: use of government spending and taxes

topics.title: Revenue receipts: taxes and non-tax revenue

learn.hook: When you pay GST on a cricket bat and your parent pays income tax, both rupees land in the same place: the government's revenue receipts.
points: Revenue receipts are receipts that neither create a liability nor reduce an asset of the government. They are non-redeemable.
Tax revenue: direct taxes are paid by the person on whom they are imposed (personal income tax, corporation tax); indirect taxes can be shifted to others (GST, customs duties, excise duties).
Progressive taxation: tax rate rises as income rises. It reduces inequality and supports the redistribution function.

Non-tax revenue: interest on loans given by the government, dividends and profits from public sector undertakings, fees, fines, and grants received from foreign governments and international organisations.
GST (introduced on 1 July 2017) replaced many indirect taxes of the Centre and States.

example.q: Classify: (i) corporation tax; (ii) GST on a mobile phone; (iii) dividends from a PSU; (iv) a passport fee.
steps: (i) paid by companies on their profits, cannot be shifted → direct tax
(ii) collected from buyers through prices → indirect tax
(iii) earnings from government investment → non-tax revenue
(iv) payment for a service → non-tax revenue (fee)
example.answer: (i) direct tax, (ii) indirect tax, (iii) and (iv) non-tax revenue

learn.reallife: Profits that the RBI and PSUs such as Coal India pass to the Centre form a large part of non-tax revenue.

neither create liabilities nor reduce assets

The tax is indirect

quiz.q: Grants received by the government from an international organisation are a

steps: Grants create no liability (not repayable) and reduce no asset
So they are revenue receipts (non-tax revenue)
Answer: revenue receipt

quiz.q: Assertion (A): GST is an indirect tax. Reason (R): The burden of GST is passed on to the final consumer through prices.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

R: its burden is passed on to consumers through prices — true

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Interest received by the government on loans given to states is a capital receipt. Reason (R): Interest receipts do not create any liability for the government.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Since interest creates no liability and reduces no asset, it is a revenue (non-tax) receipt; A is false.

So it is a revenue (non-tax) receipt, not capital: A is false
R is true
Answer: A is false, but R is true

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Where does the government get its everyday income from?'

revise.summary: Revenue receipts neither create liabilities nor reduce assets. They are tax revenue (direct taxes like income and corporation tax; indirect taxes like GST and customs) and non-tax revenue (interest, dividends, fees, fines, grants).
remember: Revenue receipt: no liability, no reduction in assets
Direct: income tax, corporation tax; indirect: GST, customs, excise
Non-tax: interest, dividends, fees, fines, grants
GST from 1 July 2017

learn.hook: Paying a teacher's salary keeps a school running this year. Building a new school building gives the country an asset for decades. The budget books them very differently.
points: Revenue expenditure neither creates assets nor reduces liabilities of the government: salaries, pensions, interest payments, subsidies, and grants to state governments (even if the grants are used for creating assets).
Capital expenditure either creates assets or reduces liabilities: building roads, dams and schools, buying machinery and land, buying shares, loans given to states and PSUs, and repayment of loans.
Interest payment on debt is revenue expenditure, but repayment of the loan principal is capital expenditure.
Capital expenditure raises the economy's productive capacity; revenue expenditure maintains the normal functioning of government.

example.q: Classify: (i) interest paid on public debt; (ii) repayment of a ₹1,000 crore loan; (iii) building a metro line; (iv) fertiliser subsidy.
steps: (i) no asset, no reduction in liability → revenue expenditure
(ii) reduces liability → capital expenditure
(iii) creates an asset → capital expenditure
(iv) no asset → revenue expenditure
example.answer: (i) and (iv) revenue expenditure; (ii) and (iii) capital expenditure

learn.reallife: The Union Budget's big push for capital expenditure on highways, railways and ports is meant to build assets that raise future growth.

steps: Asset/liability test separates the two

Answer: Capital expenditure creates assets or reduces liabilities; revenue expenditure does neither

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Purchase of shares of a public sector company by the government is capital expenditure. Reason (R): It creates a financial asset for the government.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

R: shares are a financial asset for the government — true

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

steps: Subsidies create no asset and reduce no liability (R true)
So they are revenue expenditure, not capital: A is false
Answer: A is false, but R is true
quiz.mistake: Thinks large expenditures must be capital

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I tell if a government payment is revenue expenditure or capital expenditure?'
teach.praise: Tweet! If it creates an asset or reduces a liability, it's capital expenditure; otherwise, like salaries, interest and subsidies, it's revenue expenditure!
teach.nudge: Good, but what test separates the two? Think about assets and liabilities.

revise.summary: Capital expenditure creates assets or reduces liabilities (roads, shares, loans given, loan repayment); revenue expenditure does neither (salaries, pensions, interest, subsidies, grants to states).

remember: Capital expenditure: creates assets or reduces liabilities
Interest payment: revenue; repayment of principal: capital
Grants to states: revenue expenditure

learn.hook: When the government borrows ₹1 lakh crore, it gets cash today but owes it tomorrow. When it sells part of a PSU, it gets cash but owns less. Both are capital receipts.
points: Capital receipts either create a liability or reduce an asset of the government.

Debt-creating capital receipts: borrowings from the public (market loans), from the RBI and banks (treasury bills), loans from foreign governments and international bodies, and small savings such as post office deposits.
Non-debt-creating capital receipts: recovery of loans given earlier, and disinvestment proceeds (sale of shares in public sector undertakings).
Classification test: (1) Does it create a liability or reduce an asset? Then capital. (2) Neither? Then revenue.
Recovery of a loan is a capital receipt (reduces an asset), but interest on the loan is a revenue receipt.

example.q: Classify: (i) borrowing ₹500 crore from the market; (ii) ₹200 crore from selling shares of a PSU; (iii) ₹50 crore interest from states; (iv) ₹100 crore loan repaid by a state.
steps: (i) creates a liability → debt-creating capital receipt
(ii) reduces an asset → non-debt capital receipt
(iii) no liability, no asset reduction → revenue receipt
(iv) reduces an asset (the claim on the state) → non-debt capital receipt
example.answer: (i) debt capital receipt; (ii) and (iv) non-debt capital receipts; (iii) revenue receipt

learn.reallife: Disinvestment, such as selling part of the government's stake in a company like LIC through an IPO, is a non-debt capital receipt.

learn.hook: Each Budget Day, TV anchors quote one number above all: the fiscal deficit as a percentage of GDP. Here's how it is calculated.
points: Balanced budget: estimated receipts = expenditure. Surplus budget: receipts > expenditure. Deficit budget: expenditure > receipts.
Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts. It shows government dissaving: borrowing to meet current (consumption) needs.
Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt-creating capital receipts). It equals the government's total borrowing requirement.
Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments. It shows borrowing needed for current needs apart from paying interest on past debt.
Fiscal deficit can also be written as: revenue deficit + capital expenditure − non-debt capital receipts.

example.q: Revenue receipts = 800, revenue expenditure = 1,000, capital expenditure = 200, non-debt capital receipts = 50, interest payments = 150 (₹ crore). Find RD, FD and PD.
steps: Total expenditure = 1,000 + 200 = 1,200
example.answer: RD ₹200 crore; FD ₹350 crore; PD ₹200 crore

learn.reallife: Union Budgets set fiscal deficit targets as a percentage of GDP, and rating agencies watch whether the government meets them.

topics.title: Deficits, debt and the FRBM Act

learn.hook: Borrowing to pay interest on old borrowing is like using one credit card to pay another. Governments worry about this debt trap too.
points: Fiscal deficit is financed by borrowing (from the public, banks, abroad) or, in deficit financing, by borrowing from the RBI, which creates new money and can be inflationary.
High fiscal deficits raise public debt and future interest payments. Higher interest payments raise revenue expenditure and the revenue deficit, which can lead to a debt trap.
Heavy government borrowing can push up interest rates and crowd out private investment.
The revenue deficit is a part of the fiscal deficit: FD = RD + (capital expenditure − non-debt capital receipts). A high share of RD in FD means borrowing is used for consumption, not asset creation.

The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003 set rules for fiscal discipline: reduce fiscal and revenue deficits over time (with a fiscal deficit target of 3% of GDP) and improve transparency.

example.q: FD = 1,000, of which RD = 700 (₹ crore). What share of borrowing is used for current consumption? Is this a good sign?
steps: 70% of borrowing finances revenue expenditure

learn.reallife: When interest payments take a large share of the Centre's revenue receipts, less is left for health and education; this is why fiscal discipline laws like the FRBM Act exist.
